newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Economists laud Bank Negara's improved performance.
newsitem.headline: Economists laud Bank Negara's improved performance.

text.p: Bank Negara Malaysia, long considered one of Southeast Asia's least effective central banks, has come a long way in tidying up its image, according to an informal poll of economists.
"Bank Negara has become a much more responsible central bank than in the early days," Song Seng Wun, regional economist at HG Asia Securities said on Monday.
Economists said Bank Negara's current grip on monetary policy was a far cry from the early 1990s when the central bank racked up huge losses through its speculative foreign exchange dealings.

"Over the past year, Bank Negara has been particularly impressive. It has been able to maintain a tight monetary policy despite the heavy flow of funds into the region," said Desmond Supple, Southeast Asia economist with research firm I.D.E.A.
Supple said the policy had helped slow domestic demand against the backdrop of an overheating economy and served to reduce the country's current account deficit.

While most economists ranked the tightly regulated Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) predictably near the top, the Bank of Thailand and Bank Indonesia were also viewed as skilled in managing exchange rates and capital flows.

"The Bank of Thailand knows how to use both the correct mix of the overnight rate and intervention. It's more skilled than most market players, which do not have such long institutional memories," said a senior economist with a large investment fund.
He said top management at the MAS, the Bank of Thailand and Bank Negara shared a similar level of technical expertise.

The effectiveness of Singapore's de facto central bank stemmed largely from its use of the exchange rate as a tool in controlling inflation and from the government's willingness to make tough policy choices, he said.
"They've been more inclined to control inflation than allow a little more growth at the expense of a little more inflation," he said.
Pardy Kendy, chief treasurer of PT Bank Buana Indonesia in Jakarta, pointed out that the MAS also did not have to deal with heavy offshore speculation in its currency, unlike Bank Indonesia.
"If you look at the rupiah, 70 percent of the volume is generated offshore and only some 30 percent locally. People out there in Singapore are among the most active players," he said.

Bank Indonesia's moves last week to widen the dollar/rupiah trading band to eight percent from five percent and raise the minimum reserve requirement for banks effective from April 1997 drew widespread praise from economists.

Song of HG Asia said the Indonesian central bank clearly recognised the benefits of a more flexible exchange rate policy, and by widening the band, it had reduced the need to resort to costly interventions.
"The depreciation policy is something the politicians talk about quite a lot but within the central bank corridors of power, it's not really a goal," he said.
In contrast, he said the Bank of Thailand and the Philippine central bank, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP), remained bound by the policy of keeping exchange rates within a targeted band.
But Joey Cuyegkeng, research head at Baring Securities in Manila, said the PSB had been prudent to cut back on monetary growth at the height of inflation.
"Without them, the peso would have strengthened to 24 to a U.S. dollar. They were able to enhance international reserves and make investors more comfortable," he said.
